concepts.excerpt: Centuries before the Tantric movement codified the deity-yoga move where the practitioner identifies as the deity rather than worshipping the deity from outside, a short prose text was tucked into Book 15 of the Atharvaveda.

concepts.title: The Zurxāne: The House of Strength

concepts.title: Varzeš-e Pahlavāni: The Heroic Sport

concepts.title: Košti-ye Pahlavāni: Champion Belt-Wrestling
concepts.excerpt: Every exercise in the Iranian house of strength — the push-ups, the clubs, the footwork, the whirling, the bow, the shields — exists for one thing: košti, the wrestling that crowns the practice.

concepts.excerpt: Picture a settled pastoral society on the Bronze Age steppe — herders, families, the slow work of keeping cattle alive.

concepts.excerpt: Some gods are born; this one was promoted from an adjective. "Ahura Mazdā" means "Wise Lord" — and it began life not as a name but as an epithet, a description attached to an older god (Vourunā/Varuṇa).

concepts.title: Yasna: Sacrifice & the Holy Men
concepts.excerpt: The ancient Iranians built nothing for their gods. No temples, no statues, no idols.

concepts.title: Zoroastrianism: From Zarathuštrianism to State Religion

concepts.title: Ātar & the Five Fires
concepts.excerpt: Most of the gods in this tradition live on one level — sky, atmosphere, or earth.

concepts.title: The Three Great Sacred Fires
concepts.excerpt: Pre-Islamic Iran kept three great fires burning, never let to go out, each housed in its own temple, each protecting the land from evil.

concepts.title: Apām Napāt: The Burning Water
concepts.excerpt: Here's a paradox the Iranians built a god out of: a fire that burns in water.

concepts.excerpt: In 1090, a single severe and brilliant man named Hasan-i Sabbāh captured a mountain fortress called Alamūt — "the Eagle's Nest" — in the Alborz mountains north of Tehran, and from it his small order, the Nizārī Ismāʿīlīs, waged a guerrilla war against the vast Saljūq Turkish empire for nearly two hundred years.

concepts.title: The Luṭis: The Godly Strongmen
concepts.excerpt: The word luṭi started as an insult. It meant "bandit," "vagabond" — the rough lower-class men of the 19th-century Persian streets, fruit-peddlers and drink-sellers who could fight.

concepts.title: Šeno: The Sword-Base Push-Up Sequence

concepts.title: Narmeš & Xamgiri: The Mobility Drills

concepts.title: The Mil: The Wooden Clubs
concepts.excerpt: The most recognizable image of the Iranian house of strength is a man swinging a pair of heavy, bowling-pin-shaped wooden clubs over his shoulders to the beat of a drum.

concepts.title: Milbāzi: Club Juggling
concepts.excerpt: After the heavy club-swinging is done, some Iranian houses of strength allow a spectacular display: milbāzi, "mil playing" — the juggling of two, three, or even six light clubs at once, thrown and spun and caught in complex patterns, performed solo in the center of the go'd while everyone else watches.

concepts.title: Pā Zadan: The Footwork
concepts.excerpt: After the clubs come the feet.

concepts.title: Čarx: The Whirling
concepts.excerpt: When an Iranian soldier was surrounded — outnumbered, no escape, enemies on every side — he had a last resort: take up two swords and spin, whirling in place to cut down as many of the encircling enemies as he could before he fell.

concepts.title: The Kabbāde: The Singing Steel Bow
concepts.excerpt: The Iranian house of strength has a tool that looks like a war-bow but can never fire an arrow: the kabbāde, a steel or iron bow, sixty inches long, weighing up to fifty pounds, with — instead of a bowstring — a chain hung with metal coins.

concepts.title: The Sang: The Shields of Power
concepts.excerpt: The heaviest tool in the Iranian house of strength is a pair of huge wooden shields — up to 220 pounds the pair — that you press upward off your chest while lying flat on your back, over and over, until you physically cannot continue.

concepts.title: Širin Kari: Individual Flourish Within the Collective
